extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in computer science and mathematics who are learning how to write papers, books, and expository material
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing research papers, survey articles, technical reports, proofs, and expository writing in computer science and mathematics, with attention to audience, structure, style, and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_slavish_imitation_but_don't_avoid_influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't slavishly imitate another's style, but don't avoid it either. Know the market, know thyself, and work out a compromise of your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to follow crowd trends when they're 'going in the right direction'. Imitation as influence is fine; wholesale copying of expression is not. Balance personal voice with conventions of the intended venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism_threshold_and_copyright_limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation becomes culpable if a reasonable person could not believe that you didn't have the other chap's book open in front of you as you wrote yours. You can't copyright ideas, only ways of expressing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid quoting or lifting consecutive material (e.g., a dozen successive equations) without attribution. Use explicit quotation when in doubt. Survey papers may include verbatim quotes if the writer is clearly presenting others' work; be explicit in attribution to avoid accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second_editions_and_reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Second and subsequent editions still consume significant time, though they go faster if earlier examples can be reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of real financial advantages: a new edition restarts sales lifecycle. Reuse earlier material prudently — update and revise rather than blindly recycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't_write_unless_you_are_excited
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have one thing to say about writing a paper for publication: Don't. The market is flooded. Why add to the detritus?" — Only publish for a good reason; the good reason Leslie recognizes is: 'You have done something that you are excited about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing simply to increase publication counts or to get into a specific conference. Prioritize significance and genuine contribution over opportunistic publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_bad_reasons_for_publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two bad reasons: 'to have a long publications list' and 'to have a paper published in a specific conference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing for CV padding or to get into proceedings can lead to sloppy work and dissemination of inaccurate information. Let integrity and the work's quality be the deciding factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose_publication_venue_by_readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal articles should be polished and timeless. Conference papers can be a little rougher and are appropriate for work 'not yet ready for the archives.' Technical reports are good for work not ready for the general world but still should be written up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readers and future reuse (a tech report may later become a journal article). Match the venue to the maturity and purpose of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_conceits_and_themes_judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceit (a fanciful or cute idea around which a paper can be built) can be a good catalyst but should be abandoned if it intrudes on presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Themes can help organize exposition early on but must not overshadow content or become dated (avoid jokes that age poorly). Prioritize clarity over cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_examples_over_dry_abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to have one solid example than to have a dry, abstract, academic paper. Examples keep you honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple examples (especially for lectures); ensure the theory can handle the examples you want to use. A counterexample or test example may force revision of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix_the_idea_before_polishing_sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing concern that people often 'fix the sentence and not the idea,' Leslie warned against being overly concerned with details too early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on structure and correctness of ideas first ('Don't think about format. Do think about structure.'). Formatting and micro-edits come later; ensure the concept is sound before surface edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure_over_formatting_and_use_macros
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't think about formatting when writing; think about structure. For complex notation, use a macro rather than writing it out each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in structural clarity (e.g., organizing proofs) and use typesetting tools/macros to reduce cognitive load and enforce consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_structured_statement-reason_proofs_to_clarify
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabular 'statement-reason' proofs (like high-school geometry proofs) can be much easier to read and help clarify proofs intended for paragraph presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft proofs in a structured form to check logical flow, then convert to paragraph form if desired. The handout shows an example and a trimmed bloated-prose version.

rubrics_metrics.name: First_sentence_should_be_exciting_and_nontechnical
rubrics_metrics.description: You should be excited about what you are writing and that excitement should show. First sentences can be expected to be nontechnical and to represent an author's best effort. 'Avoid passive wimpiness; be simple and direct. Get right down to business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a strong opening that 'leaps out'. The first sentence sets reader expectations; follow with equally strong subsequent sentences to maintain engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain_reader_engagement_throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: If you hit readers 'in the gut' with your first sentence, you can't let them down with the second; by induction you must keep delivering quality throughout the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain clarity, novelty, and interest through the entire exposition — not just the opening. Avoid slippage later in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition_equals_organisation_plus_simplification_plus_joy
rubrics_metrics.description: For Nilsson, composition = Organisation + Simplification + Joy. Writing should be both art and communication, charged with artistic passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to organize material clearly, simplify presentation where useful, and enjoy the craft so that passion appears in the writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start_early_and_rewrite_relentlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Start early. Rewrite, rewrite, rewrite... It is the extremely rare artist who does not need to labour over and over on his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat early drafts as sketches to discard; multiple revisions are essential. Expect to iterate many times before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get_peer_critique_before_publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let anything you write be published without having had others critique it. A university environment is good for feedback, but time requests carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit knowledgeable readers, be receptive to corrections (examples: McCarthy/Lifschitz finding oversights), and revise accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn_to_write_by_reading_widely
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning to write is more like learning to play the piano than learning to type; a good writer must spend much time studying great literature and reading widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read authors across genres (including great literature) to develop style, phrasing, and rhetorical sense that improve mathematical and technical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model_the_reader_and_anticipate_misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the reader: ask 'How is the reader going to misunderstand me here?' and develop background 'daemons' (automatic checks) to catch errors and stylistic slips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train heuristics that run unconsciously while writing (e.g., flag split infinitives, inconsistent notation). Aim to anticipate and remove likely confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master_the_medium_vocabulary_and_visual_tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Master the medium: have a good vocabulary and understand other issues like indexes, tables, graphs, and typography to make important distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate typographical conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logical formulae) and visual aids to improve clarity; vocabulary needn't be large but should be precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master_the_material_through_writing_and_teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing helps you understand your material: 'The writer writes in order to teach himself, to understand himself.' Give talks and teach to refine your internal model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lecturing, talks, and organizing material into a book/paper to reveal gaps in reasoning and improve exposition; iterative feedback from teaching informs revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify_initial_presentation_then_elaborate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to present the reader with something straightforward to start off with; you can add correct details later. 'Everything should always be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple examples/versions (80-20 rule) to convey most of the idea before introducing generalizations; simplify exposition initially, then repay 'debt to truth' with elaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_recycling_old_material_without_rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: With on-line text and editors it is tempting to re-use portions of old material. Resist the temptation. You are likely writing in a new context and should rewrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rework previous text to fit new emphasis, different audience, and possibly improved style; expect to invest effort to adapt rather than copy-paste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim_for_excellence_and_continuous_improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep shooting for perfection even if you'll never get there. Be never satisfied; demand the best in everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold high standards, constantly refine, and don't accept 'good enough' when better clarity or rigor is achievable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary_exercises_and_reference_tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve command of vocabulary via exercises (swap words, write thesaurus entries). Everyone needs at least one thesaurus and a good unabridged dictionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a nuanced sense of word choice; compare personal synonym sets with authoritative references to refine usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic_mastery_over_lexical_showiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic mastery is more important than adding big words; you will usually use a basic 3–4k word vocabulary but must use it in the most interesting ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice varied sentence structures; exercises include periodic sentences, recasting sentences to change emphasis, and deliberate syntactic variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim_for_appropriate_sentence_length_and_variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mary-Claire's guideline: averages under 20 words per sentence are in the correct range for adult writing; ideal bell-curve centered around 15–18 words. With 10 sentences, aim for 9 or 10 different lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include short 'punchy' sentences and occasional long sentences used sparingly for de-emphasis; avoid monotonous sentence-length patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_repetitive_sentence_templates_and_use_parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the same sentence construction repeatedly (e.g., adverbial + subject + transitive-verb + object). Tight parallels—two adjacent sentences with exactly the same construction—are effective when used intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary syntactic templates to maintain reader interest, but learn the power of deliberate parallelism for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be_cautious_with_periodic_sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic sentences (where grammatical and physical ends coincide) are a high literary form and not generally appropriate for mathematical writing, though awareness of them helps control sentence structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve periodic constructions for specific rhetorical effects; prefer more direct sentence forms in technical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recast_sentences_to_change_emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphatic positions in a sentence are the front and the back; the middle is 'sort of a slum.' Recast sentences to move emphasis as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice varying placement of key information to control what the reader takes away from a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual_labor_techniques_to_internalize_text
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual exercises (typing out, copying in longhand, memorization, recitation) help slow reading and give text the consideration it deserves; these practices help develop 'manual' aspects of composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use copying or recitation to internalize rhythm and syntactic choices; these techniques can be surprisingly effective for noticing stylistic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read_aloud_and_pair_up_for_feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Read aloud to students/peers and form partnerships of novice writers to read and listen to each other's work. A little goes a long way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing prose reveals flaws and strengths; provide and accept concise, focused feedback to improve draft quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks_on_paper_and_iterative_editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is 'the most forgiving medium known to man.' Use marks on paper and iterative editing to see what you mean and get it right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in line-editing, structural edits, and multiple passes; don't rush finalization—use feedback and marking to guide revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance_voice_and_tone_via_exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrow techniques from speech therapy: exaggerate defects until you understand them. If someone says your style is 'breezy,' write something truly off the wall to locate the defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conscious exaggeration exercises to isolate and correct habitual tone/voice issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion_and_versification_exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Scansion exercises (writing verse) are hard but very important; they help with rhythm and prosody of prose even in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice poetic exercises to develop sensitivity to rhythm, sentence flow, and cadence in technical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precis_exercises_and_concision_constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Precis exercises demonstrate that at some point you cannot reduce word count without changing structure; you should never change meaning, but you may have to dispense with some details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice reducing text while preserving meaning; learn where structural change is required to achieve concision and which details can be omitted or deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly_real_exercises_and_exposition_practice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nearly real" exercises mimic real writing tasks; Mary-Claire notes that 'writing a joke is exposition' — these exercises are valuable practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use near-realistic composition tasks to practice exposition, pacing, and rhetoric in contexts close to intended publication or presentation.
